Exploring the Ann Arbor Arboretum to Identify Areas/Path for Running

Reading in the LAS file for the Arboretum area of Ann Arbor and assessing initial findings.

In looking at this plot, there seems to be high canopy cover in the southern area, with some high buildings to the north. A stream also seems to be flowing through the Arb which could cause a nice breeze during summer running.

plot(lasArb, bg = "white")
movie3d(spin3d(), duration = 5, movie = exportPath, webshot = F)

This shows a moving graphic of the study area, which helped me to see that there might be trees in the northern side too that I should also explore for a running path.

Exploring the Terrain of the Arboretum

Digital Terrain Modeling

Now that I have an idea of where canopy cover may be in the study site, I want to get an idea of the terrain to understand where elevation points may be. In my runs, I may want to avoid the higher elevation areas unless purposefully doing hill workouts.

# converting the las into terra dtm
dtm1 <- lidR::rasterize_terrain(lasArb, res = 1, knnidw(k = 6, p = 2), keep_lowest = F)

#plot 2d
tm_shape(dtm1)+
  tm_raster(style= "cont")+
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)

#plot 3d
plot_dtm3d(dtm1)

These two plots are very helpful. The 2D plot shows that there is steeper topography in both the southern and northeastern areas. It seems that around the river there is flatter topography, which could be a nice, flat area to run to see river views.

Below I plotted the distribution of elevation values of the area. Most of the area is on the lower end of relative elevation (between 750 and 800), which bodes well for my running. I will likely want to avoid or minimize the higher elevations areas if possible, and would want to avoid gaining elevation in too short of a distance.

dtmdf <-  as.data.frame(dtm1)

ggplot(dtmdf) +
    geom_histogram(aes(Z)) +
    xlab("DTM Elevation Value (m)") +
    ggtitle("Distribution of DTM Values")

Terrain Modeling

Rendering shaded DTM

Here I generate a hillshade raster, which simulates sunlight to create shadows/highlights that clarify topographic features. I use two different methods to do this, then plot this.

library(terra) #analysis for slope & aspect
dtm2 <- rasterize_terrain(lasArb, res = 16.4042, algorithm = kriging(k = 40))

slope <- terra::terrain(dtm2, "slope", unit="radians") 
aspect <- terra::terrain(dtm2, "aspect", unit="radians")
hs <- shade(slope, aspect, angle=45, direction=315)

tm_shape(hs)+
  tm_raster(style = "cont", palette = "Greys")+
  tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
## 
## ── tmap v3 code detected ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
## [v3->v4] `tm_raster()`: instead of `style = "cont"`, use col.scale =
## `tm_scale_continuous()`.
## ℹ Migrate the argument(s) 'palette' (rename to 'values') to
##   'tm_scale_continuous(<HERE>)'
## [cols4all] color palettes: use palettes from the R package cols4all. Run
## `cols4all::c4a_gui()` to explore them. The old palette name "Greys" is named
## "brewer.greys"

#rayshader method
library(rayshader)
elmat <- raster_to_matrix(dtm2)
map <- elmat %>%
  sphere_shade(texture = "imhof1", progbar = FALSE) %>%
  add_water(detect_water(elmat), color = "imhof1") %>%
  add_shadow(ray_shade(elmat, progbar = FALSE), 0.5) %>%
  add_shadow(ambient_shade(elmat, progbar = FALSE), 0)
plot_map(map)

plot_3d(map, elmat, zscale = 5, windowsize = c(800, 800))

These graphics show that the southern area is relatively well-shaded besides what looks like high canopy treetops and high ridges. The northern side has some light reflection on what seems to be buildings. The rayshader plot shows this a little more clearly, outlining trees and buildings better and representing contrast from shaded areas better. The rayshader plot also informs me of a railroad crossing through the area, which I had not recognized before from the previous plots. The 3D plot reaffirms these observations, and emphasizes the height/elevation differences on either side of the river. While the southern side is well-shaded so should be conducive to running, it has much higher elevation than the northern side, making my proposed running path a difficult choice.

Normalized Model

Now I want to understand the height of trees and buildings with the ground at 0, in case there are trees elsewhere that I haven’t recognized due to the elevation that would provide similar canopy cover as the southern area. To do this, I subtract the DTM from LiDAR data.

lasnorm <- normalize_height(lasArb, dtm2, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(lasnorm)

This shows that there are trees along the river and throughout the northern area that are similar heights to those in the southern area, just less populous. This shows me that I will be able to find canopy cover if I run in the northern area, while avoiding some of the high elevation, which is the best of both worlds for running! I could run on either side of the river and be happy, though would probably stick close to the river in either case to maintain a lower elevation and avoid the buildings and potential traffic in the north.

Discussion

This visualization provided new perspective on the relativity of tree height when elevation is taken into account. I also learned that something as simple as a railroad can look very indescribable when viewed from above with different color palettes, as it took me a long time to orient around what was the river and what was the railroad. My research focus showed me that the north side of the study area could be improved by tree plantings as trees are much more populous on the southern, mainly Arboretum side. However, the visualization did not provide much information about what was in the north, besides some distinguishable buildings, so there may be good reasons there are less trees than I would hope (like roads, parking lots, etc). However, I am sure that near the tall buildings and near the square, field-seeming areas that there are opportunities for tree plantings.

There are advantages and complexities of 3D geovisualization. 3D geovisualizations can facilitate learning because a user/viewer can change angles to improve understanding, helping them visualize and retain information. This makes these geovisualizations more understandable and intuitive for the general public, who may be new to whatever information the geovisualization is trying to present. However, 3D geovisualizations are also technologically complex, so creating them is not very accessible, meaning that some very important information may not be presented in the best manner because of lack of knowledge. Additionally, the exploratory nature of 3D could cause privacy or security concerns if that sort of exploratory analysis is done in sensitive areas. However, I think 3D technology is overall becoming more accessible (especially with the assistance of AI), and will become a common form of data presentation. This will be very helpful in both academic and professional environments, especially as modeling future scenarios (related to climate, landscape, urbanization, etc) becomes more important.
